props.title: Season of the Witch

sections.content: George A. Romero's Season of the Witch (1972) marks a fascinating departure from his zombie films, diving into feminist themes and suburban occultism. Released between Night of the Living Dead (1968) and The Crazies (1973), this overlooked gem captures the emerging women's liberation movement through a supernatural lens. The film's original title "Jack's Wife" better reflects its focus on Joan Mitchell's transformation from repressed housewife to empowered witch, predating similar themes in films like The Stepford Wives (1975).

sections.content: The early 1970s saw a surge in occult-themed films examining women's roles in society. While Rosemary's Baby (1968) explored patriarchal control through supernatural horror, Season of the Witch took a more nuanced approach to female empowerment through witchcraft. This theme would later influence films like The Craft (1996) and Suspiria (1977), where supernatural powers become metaphors for female agency and rebellion against societal constraints.

Romero's signature social commentary shines through the film's exploration of suburban malaise. Like his contemporary The Stepford Wives (1975), Season of the Witch critiques the suffocating nature of suburban life and traditional marriage. The film's low-budget aesthetic and documentary-style moments create an unsettling realism that makes its supernatural elements more impactful. SUBHEAD: Influence on Modern Witch Cinema

sections.content: Season of the Witch's influence can be seen in modern feminist horror like The Love Witch (2016) and The Witch (2015), which similarly explore feminine power through occult themes. The film's blend of social commentary and supernatural elements created a template for examining women's issues through genre cinema, later seen in works like Jennifer's Body (2009) and A Dark Song (2016).
